opus-5.5.text:
It's a really tempting idea, and on paper it sounds like the most direct path: find people who have the disease, find people who don't, sample their scent, and train a classifier to tell the two apart. Dogs have shown us there's real signal there, for things like certain cancers, Parkinson's, even COVID. So the premise isn't crazy.

But I think the straightforward version of that approach is actually really hard to make work, and a lot of the difficulty is statistical before it's chemical.

The first problem is that human scent is incredibly high-dimensional and incredibly noisy. What you smell like on any given day depends on what you ate, what soap you used, whether you exercised, your microbiome, your medications, the room you were sampled in, the humidity, the instrument's drift that week. The disease signal, if it exists, is a faint whisper sitting on top of an enormous amount of variance that has nothing to do with the disease. To pull that whisper out with a model trained from scratch, you need a lot of labeled examples, and labeled examples of sick people are expensive, slow, and ethically sensitive to collect.

The second problem is confounding, which is the one that really keeps me up at night. If your disease cohort was sampled at a hospital and your controls were sampled somewhere else, or at a different time, or they're on different medications because they're sick, your model will happily learn to detect the hospital, or the drug, or the batch, and it'll look fantastic on your held-out set. Then you deploy it and it falls apart. With small datasets and very flexible models, that's almost the default outcome unless you're extraordinarily careful about study design.

So my view is that disease detection is a fantastic goal, but probably the wrong place to start. The approach I find more promising is to first build a general-purpose representation of odor, a map of smell, if you will, learned from a broad base of data about how molecules relate to perception and to each other. Once you have a good representation, the downstream task of "does this person's scent profile shift in a disease-associated way" becomes a much smaller learning problem. You're fine-tuning on top of something that already understands the structure of the space, rather than asking a model to discover both the structure of olfaction and the disease signal at the same time from a few hundred samples.

It's a similar story to what happened in vision and language. People didn't get robust medical imaging models by training only on a few thousand X-rays; it got much better once there were strong pretrained representations to build on. I think olfaction needs that foundational layer first, and then the disease applications, which I think are genuinely some of the most exciting and humane uses of this technology, become tractable.

r001.rationale: The response says labeled examples are expensive, slow, and ethically sensitive to collect, and that many are needed. It does not clearly argue that direct collection cannot realistically produce enough participants.

fable-5.1.text:
So, this is something I think about a lot, because it's the obvious first move and it's also, I think, a bit of a trap if you do it naively.

The obvious version is: you go collect breath, or skin swabs, or urine from a cohort of people who have, say, Parkinson's, and a cohort who don't, you run everything through a sensor, you train a classifier, and you get a number. And the number is often really good! That's actually the problem. Because what you've frequently learned is not the disease. You've learned the hospital. You've learned that the sick people were sampled on a Tuesday in one clinic and the healthy people were sampled at a wellness fair across town. You've learned diet, medication, the soap in the bathroom, the ambient volatiles in the room. Scent is incredibly high-dimensional and incredibly leaky, so every confound you can imagine shows up in the signal, and the model will happily latch onto whatever is easiest.

So my assessment is: it's necessary, but it's not sufficient, and it's not where I'd start. The thing that makes the dog studies compelling, the ones where a dog can pick out a Parkinson's patient from a T-shirt, is that the dog is generalizing across a huge amount of uncontrolled variation. If you want a machine to do that, you either need a dataset that's enormous and genuinely diverse, collected across many sites, many seasons, with real blinding, or you need a foundation. And the foundation, for us, is understanding the chemistry itself. What does a molecule smell like? What molecules are actually present? If you have a model that has a general representation of odor space, then the disease problem becomes a much smaller fine-tuning problem on top of it, rather than trying to learn all of chemistry from a few hundred patient samples.

The other thing I'd flag is that the end-to-end, "just collect and train" approach gives you a black box at exactly the moment you need interpretability most. If a model says this person has a disease, a clinician is going to ask why, and "the sensor array lit up in pattern seven" is not an answer. If instead you can say, we see elevated levels of these specific compounds, and here's the biology that connects them to the condition, now you have something that can be validated, that can be turned into a biomarker, that can go through a regulatory process.

So I'd put it this way. Collecting data from real patients is the ground truth, and you can't skip it. But treat it as the validation step and the final mile, not as the whole project. Build the general-purpose sense of smell first, be paranoid about confounds, and make sure that whatever the model finds can be traced back to actual molecules. Otherwise you get a very impressive paper and a device that stops working the moment you move it to a different hospital.

r001.rationale: The response says a few hundred patient samples are insufficient to learn all of chemistry and calls for enormous, diverse data or a general odor model. It does not argue that directly collecting from people cannot realistically yield enough participants.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a reasonable place to start, but the hard part is knowing what your model actually learned. If you collect samples from people with a disease in a hospital and your healthy controls somewhere else, you might build a very good hospital detector. You could also be picking up medications, diet, or differences in how the samples were collected and stored.

So you need to design the collection very carefully, and then test on people from a different site, ideally at a different time, with the model fixed. Does the signal still hold up? And does it distinguish the disease from other conditions that look similar, rather than just distinguish sick people from healthy people?

You don’t necessarily have to understand every molecule to build a useful predictor. But I’d be much more confident if we could connect the scent signal to the underlying biology. Collecting the data is a starting point; establishing that you’ve captured something specific and reproducible about the disease is the real challenge.

r001.rationale: The response calls direct collection a reasonable starting point and discusses confounding and validation, but does not argue that it cannot realistically yield enough participants to train a strong model.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a promising approach, but the hard part is knowing what your model has actually learned. If you collect samples from people with a disease in a hospital and samples from healthy people somewhere else, you might build a very good detector of the hospital environment rather than the disease.

So you have to be careful about how you collect the samples and what else differs between those groups—medications, diet, things like that. Then you need to test on people and samples collected independently. The question is whether there’s a signal that generalizes beyond the particular group you started with. Collecting the data is essential, but getting that experimental design right is what makes the result meaningful.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls direct scent-data collection promising and emphasizes confounding and independent testing; it does not argue that participant numbers are insufficient to train a strong model.
